title: Young Women Fuel Sharp Rise in Type 2 Diabetes Across England, Study Finds
excerpt: A landmark Imperial College London analysis reveals early-onset type 2 diabetes diagnoses are surging among women under 40, driven by escalating obesity rates in younger generations.
body:
• Type 2 diabetes diagnoses rose 69% in women aged 20–29 in England between 2011 and 2024, while declining in older age groups.
  • BMI at diagnosis climbed roughly twice as fast in younger adults compared to those over 40, with some groups approaching severe obesity thresholds.
  • The increase spans all ethnicities and is not confined to minority populations, according to the first nationwide analysis of its kind.
  • Researchers are calling for earlier interventions, including expanded access to GLP-1 medications and weight-management programmes for younger adults.

Young women under 40 are driving a rapid increase in early-onset type 2 diabetes across England, according to a major new analysis that reveals a stark generational divide in how the disease is spreading.

The study, published in Lancet Regional Health Europe and led by Indian-origin researcher Dr. Shivani Misra at Imperial College London, is the first to examine trends in new type 2 diabetes diagnoses across England's entire population while breaking down the data by age, sex, and ethnicity.

A Generational Split

Researchers analysed data from the English National Diabetes Audit covering 2011 to 2024 and found a clear pattern: diagnoses are rising sharply among adults under 40, even as they fall in those over 60.

The age-standardised incidence of type 2 diabetes rose by 43% in men and 69% in women aged 20 to 29 over the study period. Women aged 20 to 39 saw an annual increase of roughly 3% in diagnosis rates. By contrast, both men and women aged 60 to 79 saw rates decline by about 2% per year.

"We have known for a long time that obesity is linked to type 2 diabetes, but what is new from this study is the scale of the change occurring in younger adults."

— Dr. Shivani Misra, Imperial College London

The findings carry particular weight because early-onset type 2 diabetes leads to longer lifetime exposure to the disease, earlier death, and a greater risk of serious complications, including poor pregnancy outcomes.

Obesity Rising Faster in the Young

The study also revealed that body mass index at the time of diagnosis has been climbing far more steeply among younger adults. Between 2011 and 2024, BMI at diagnosis rose by 5% to 7% in adults under 40, compared with just 2% to 3% in those aged 40 and over. White women diagnosed at younger ages had average BMIs approaching 40 kg/m² — a threshold classified as severe obesity.

"We think that the earlier onset of severe obesity in young people is increasing their type 2 diabetes risk in early life and pulling down their age at diagnosis," Misra told The Telegraph. "This is really worrying given the poor health outcomes from early-onset type 2 diabetes."

Not Just an Ethnic Minority Problem

Previous discussions around rising type 2 diabetes in younger people have focused heavily on ethnic minority groups. But the Imperial analysis shows the increase is far broader. The rise is particularly noticeable among white, Asian, and Black women aged 20 to 29, and among white women aged 30 to 39.

"While these ethnic groups are disproportionately affected by early-onset type 2 diabetes, we now see that incidence is also increasing in white populations, showing that this public health challenge is broadening across the generation," Misra said.

For South Asians, the findings add to a body of research showing they develop type 2 diabetes at lower BMIs than white Europeans, partly due to greater genetic susceptibility to poor beta cell function — the cells in the pancreas responsible for producing insulin. Britain is home to roughly 1.5 million people of South Asian descent, many of whom face elevated risk even without the severe obesity seen in other groups.

Calls for Earlier Intervention

The authors argue that current diabetes prevention strategies are failing younger generations. They recommend earlier identification of at-risk individuals, expanded participation in prevention programmes at younger ages, earlier use of GLP-1 medications — the class of drugs that includes semaglutide — and targeted weight-management support, including intensive lifestyle interventions and bariatric surgery for those with severe obesity.

Helen Kirrane, head of policy at Diabetes UK, said the rise in type 2 diabetes among younger adults is "deeply concerning." She called on the government to restrict the promotion of unhealthy food and create environments that support healthier lives.

What's Next

The NHS has already begun responding. Its T2Day programme, backed by £14.5 million in funding, targets roughly 140,000 people aged 18 to 39 with additional health checks and tailored diabetes management. The programme was co-developed by Misra and addresses the added risks the condition poses during pregnancy.

The researchers are urging that age-stratified analyses become standard practice in assessing diabetes trends, arguing that national averages can mask critical shifts within specific population groups. With 4.7 million diabetes diagnoses in the UK — 90% of them type 2 — the stakes of missing those shifts are high.
